paras: The Lonoke whitecapping shooting was a night attack in June 1903 in which masked white men with shotguns fired into a camp of three Black timber cutters about five miles from Lonoke, Arkansas. One of the men, called Bob Anderson in the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic and Bob Armstrong in a later state news item, was reported killed, though the first briefs said only that he was thought or believed to have died. Three white farmers were arrested on a charge of white-capping and held to the grand jury, and Arkansas papers presented the case as an effort by Lonoke's "better element" to end whitecapping.

According to a Lonoke telegram to the Little Rock Gazette, reprinted in the Graphic, whitecapping had "been going on near there for some years." The band blamed for it was said to refuse to allow a Black person to work or live in that vicinity or in the adjacent neighborhoods. The three men in the camp were cutting timber, and the two survivors said John Weaver had given them permission to cut at that spot.

The shooting took place after 10 o'clock on a Monday night, which by the dates of the reports was 8 June 1903. Morris East and Jim Scott, both about twenty-five, said the masked attackers fired four times at Scott and repeatedly at East, and that Anderson had taken off his shoes for bed when the firing began. The Sharp County Record said they were tie makers asleep in a cabin.

Anderson's shoes were later found at a foot-log a mile away, and the Gazette correspondent wrote that the whitecappers were thought to have put them there. No report of a body being found or of an inquest appears in the coverage.

When the news reached Lonoke, Judge George W. Chapline, the attorney Joe T. Robinson, Sheriff A. J. Wallis and his deputies, and about fifty citizens went to the scene to search. The sheriff (also printed Wall and Walls) jailed two farmers, W. P. Trimble and Bill Counts, and the next morning arrested a third, J. A. Wilcox, in Lonoke. In jail, Counts told a Gazette reporter he was not guilty and had heard the shooting nearly a mile away, and Trimble said gunfire near his house had woken him.

Robinson, called one of the state's leading attorneys, agreed to push the prosecution although the prisoners had wanted to retain him. Lonoke residents raised money by private subscription to prosecute, and after a preliminary hearing the accused were held to the grand jury. No report of an indictment or trial was found.
The raid frightened many Black laborers, who left the community, and the Graphic reported that many had abandoned their crops.

All the coverage found came from white Arkansas papers between 14 and 24 June 1903; no Black newspaper account was found. The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic first noted it in a one-sentence brief about a "kuklux band," then on 15 June ran the Gazette's Lonoke telegram under the headline "KUKLUXING IN LONOKE: Good Citizens Are Determined to Put a Stop to It." That account called the dead man "a harmless old darkey" and dwelt on the town's reputation, saying citizens were determined that "the good name of the town shall not suffer from such affairs."

A shorter item headed "Alleged White Cappers Arrested" ran in the Monticellonian on 18 June and in identical form in the Newark Journal and the Forrest City Times on 19 June and the Malvern Times-Journal on 24 June. It framed the case as a matter of labor, saying the "better element of citizens" had decided to punish all who "intimidate laborers." The Sharp County Record called it "the outrage" and, like the others, gave most of its space to the arrests and the plans to prosecute.

The Graphic's account, drawn from interviews with the survivors in Lonoke, names the dead man Bob Anderson, who had lived there with his family for twenty years, while the Monticellonian names him Bob Armstrong, "a harmless old man." The early briefs said only that one man was thought or believed killed, the Monticellonian stated the killing flatly, and the Graphic reports his shoes but no body.

accounts.label: Gazette correspondent at Lonoke (via Pine Bluff Daily Graphic)
accounts.gist: Whitecappers shot into a Black camp five miles out on Monday night; a band that bars Black people from the area was supposed to have taken the life of Bob Anderson; three farmers arrested.

accounts.label: Survivors Morris East and Jim Scott
accounts.gist: Masked men with shotguns fired repeatedly at them; Anderson had his shoes off preparing for bed; they had permission from John Weaver to cut timber there.

accounts.label: Accused farmers
accounts.gist: Counts said he was not guilty and heard the shots nearly a mile away; Trimble said he was asleep nearby, woken by the guns, and saw no one pass.

accounts.label: State news item
accounts.gist: A crowd of white men shot into a camp of timber cutters, killing Bob Armstrong; laborers fled; the better element hired counsel to prosecute.

framing.detail: Pine Bluff Daily Graphic headline 'KUKLUXING IN LONOKE / Good Citizens Are Determined to Put a Stop to It', calling it 'disgraceful conduct' and the victim 'a harmless old darkey', with stress on Lonoke's good name.
'Alleged White Cappers Arrested' item, run in several Arkansas weeklies, framed the case as intimidation of laborers that the 'better element' would punish.
Sharp County Record state column called it 'the outrage' and noted money raised to prosecute.

conflicts.note: The Graphic's account rests on a Lonoke correspondent who interviewed the survivors and is the more local and detailed; the Armstrong item is a later digest.

versions.value: band 'took the life' of Anderson; only his shoes found, a mile away

conflicts.note: No report of a body or inquest appears.
